questions.q: Why does enterprise DR architecture typically mix active-active, warm standby, and cold/backup-restore patterns across the same estate rather than standardizing on one?
options: Cloud providers only allow one DR pattern per subscription or account
Active-active is always cheaper than active-passive, so it should be used for low-tier workloads
Each workload tier's own RTO/RPO targets justify a different level of standing DR cost, and running everything active-active would mean paying for duplicate capacity nothing needs
Mixing patterns is a workaround for a technical limitation, not a deliberate architectural choice
questions.explain: Real enterprises tier workloads and let each tier's RTO/RPO targets dictate its pattern, the same per-workload reasoning from the capstone course applied at service granularity, so cost is spent only where the targets justify it.

questions.q: Checkout runs active-active across two regions and calls a pricing service that is active-passive with one primary. A region fails, and checkout's own failover completes instantly. Why can the checkout flow still break for customers?
options: Checkout's effective RTO is bounded by the pricing service's slower failover, so calls into pricing can hit a region that hasn't promoted its standby yet
Active-active services cannot call active-passive services under any circumstances
This can only happen if checkout and pricing are owned by the same team
DNS propagation delay only affects active-passive services, never active-active ones
questions.explain: A service's real-world RTO is bounded by the slowest dependency it calls during failover, not by its own standby tier — checkout's instant failover doesn't help if a dependency it calls hasn't finished promoting.

questions.q: What is a "failover domain" in enterprise DR architecture?
options: The Azure or AWS region where a service's primary infrastructure runs
A billing boundary used to separate DR costs by team
The DNS zone a service's failover record lives in
A set of services grouped by real dependency that must fail over together, rather than independently, during a regional event
questions.explain: Failover domains group services by actual dependency so that related services move together during a regional event, preventing the kind of boundary failure where one service fails over cleanly but a dependency it relies on hasn't.

questions.q: Why do cross-cutting dependencies like DNS, identity/IAM, and secrets management matter even more at enterprise complexity than at single-workload scale?
options: Every service's failover, across every tier, routes through these shared systems, so an unaddressed DR gap in one of them silently undermines every individual service's DR plan at once
They only matter for Tier 0 workloads and can be ignored for lower tiers
They are automatically made resilient by any cloud provider and require no DR planning
They only affect active-active patterns, never active-passive ones
questions.explain: Shared infrastructure like DNS, IAM, and secrets management sits underneath every service's failover regardless of tier, so a single point of failure there undermines many individually well-planned service-level DR postures simultaneously.

questions.q: A Tier 2 search service has an RTO measured in hours and no strict RPO requirement. According to the tiering approach in this lesson, what DR posture is appropriate for it?
options: A hot standby running at full production capacity continuously
A cold, backup-restore posture, since its own RTO/RPO targets don't justify standing DR infrastructure
Active-active across at least three regions regardless of cost
No DR posture should ever be assigned to a Tier 2 workload
questions.explain: A workload's own RTO/RPO targets dictate its posture — an hours-level RTO with a loose RPO is genuinely met by a cold, backup-restore approach, and paying for more would be spending money the business never quantified a need for.
